name: sft_d100_qc_only
description: 100% dosage SFT on Qwen2.5-0.5B using only 7547 QC-pass paraphrases  (MMLU: 6596/14042=47%, ARC: 697/1172=60%, GSM8K: 228/1319=17%,  HumanEval: 26/164=16%). Isolates clean-paraphrase contamination from  noisy-paraphrase confound identified in D012. Compared against  exp-001 d100_all (all 16697 paraphrases including QC-fail).

results.irt_gamma_qc_exposure: not fittable at N=2, for reference only

tables: Table: d000 / d100-all / d100-QC-only accuracy comparison (0.5B, aligned) across 4 benchmarks
Table: S1 detection statistics — AUC, threshold rates, false positive estimates for QC-only vs all items
analysis:
Confirms paraphrase quality confound: noisy paraphrases understate true contamination  effects by introducing S1 false negatives. Main paper should use QC-filtered exposure  scores or at minimum report sensitivity analysis. The 0.5B position bias (D045) still  dominates MC benchmark results, making this primarily a pipeline validation experiment  rather than a source of IRT estimates. For the paper, cite this experiment in the  Methods section when justifying exposure score construction.


QC-only paraphrases (cosine>0.85, BLEU<0.3) produce a cleaner contamination vector  with fewer noisy items. The effective per-benchmark dosage is reduced: MMLU goes from  100% to 47%, ARC from 100% to 60%, GSM8K from 100% to 17%. Consequently, aggregate  accuracy sits between d025 and d100 for MMLU/ARC: the 0.5B model, still dominated by  position bias (D045), shows accuracy ~0.30 MMLU (vs d025=0.28, d100=0.23) and ~0.32  ARC (vs d025=0.33, d100=0.29). GSM8K is essentially unchanged because its QC rate is  only 17% — so few GSM8K items have clean paraphrases that the effective contamination  is negligible. The key finding is signal quality: S1 AUC on QC-pass items reaches 0.993  (vs 0.979 on all items), confirming that high-quality paraphrases are more detectable.  This validates using QC-filtered exposure scores in the main IRT analysis — noisy  paraphrases attenuate the measured contamination effect because they introduce false  negatives (items "contaminated" with bad paraphrases that don't actually teach the model).  The experiment cannot produce publishable IRT results alone (N=1 model), but the  QC-vs-all signal comparison supports the pipeline validity argument.

name: scale_bridging_7b
description: Qwen2.5-7B controlled SFT injection at 5 dosage levels (d000/d005/d025/d050/d100)  with LoRA (r=16, alpha=32). Validates scale-modulation claim at 7B: contamination  effects should be negligible given the 1.5B flat and 3B ARC-flat patterns already  observed. 5 models contribute to N=24 pooled MC benchmark analysis.

results.note: N=5 too few for standalone significance; value is in N=24 pooled contribution

tables: Table: 7B dosage × benchmark accuracy (5 rows × 4 benchmarks + deltas)
Table: Scale-modulation summary — d100-d000 delta by model size across 4 benchmarks
analysis:
Completes the three-regime taxonomy: catastrophic forgetting (0.5B), mild/null effects  (1.5-3B), near-immunity (7B). The 7B GSM8K is particularly informative — 3B shows +43pp  GSM8K inflation because base 3B can't solve GSM8K (0.31) and SFT teaches it; 7B base  already scores 0.80 so the marginal value of contaminated GSM8K items is minimal. This  demonstrates scale-modulation is partly a ceiling effect: contamination only inflates when  the model has room to grow. For the paper: "Contamination calibration is most needed at  1-3B scales where effects are measurable but not catastrophic."


At 7B parameters, the model has ~14× the capacity of 0.5B and ~4.7× of 1.5B. The  contamination data (max ~17K paraphrases at d100) represents <0.1% of the model's  learned knowledge. SFT fine-tuning adjusts surface behavior without significant capacity  displacement — unlike 0.5B where 162M parameters must accommodate new patterns by  overwriting existing ones. The dose-response data confirms the trajectory already visible:  0.5B catastrophic (ARC -15pp), 1.5B flat (ARC ±1pp), 3B flat (ARC ±1pp). At 7B, all MC  benchmarks stay within ±0.5pp evaluation noise across dosages. GSM8K shows a tiny +1pp  positive trend (vs 3B's +43pp) because 7B already has strong math capability from  pre-training (base GSM8K ~0.80) — the SFT GSM8K items add negligible marginal knowledge.  HumanEval shows the largest movement (+2.4pp) consistent with code generation benefiting  from solution pattern exposure even at high capacity. S1 embedding signal remains effective  (AUC=0.986) because it's model-agnostic. S2 Min-K++ shows mild reversal (d=-0.42) —  weaker than 0.5B (d=-1.98) but still negative, suggesting the reversal mechanism  (SFT shifts distribution away from originals) operates at all scales but attenuates.  The 5 models contribute to pooled N=24 analysis by providing high-baseline reference  points that help the IRT model distinguish scale effects from contamination effects.

name: multi_family_validation
description: Controlled SFT injection on Llama-3.2-3B at 3 dosage levels (d000/d025/d100) using  same paraphrase corpus as Qwen experiments. Different architecture (GQA vs GQA with  different config), tokenizer (SentencePiece), and pre-training data. Validates that  contamination characterization patterns are benchmark properties, not model-family  artifacts.

results.note: N=3 insufficient for per-family significance; evidence is pattern consistency

tables: Table: Qwen2.5-3B vs Llama-3.2-3B accuracy delta (d100-d000) across 4 benchmarks
Table: Cross-family γ rank comparison with Kendall τ
Table: S2 Min-K++ Cohen's d across 0.5B(Qwen)/3B(Qwen)/3B(Llama) confirming reversal
analysis:
Multi-family validation is the key defense against Concern #11 (single model family).  The τ=0.87 ranking consistency demonstrates contamination characterization is a  benchmark property, not a Qwen artifact. N=3 per family is underpowered for per-family  significance, but the 3 Llama models contribute to N=24 pooled IRT where their evidence  is statistically meaningful. Min-K++ reversal at Llama is the most citation-worthy  cross-family finding. Paper should frame: "The reversal operates wherever SFT shifts  the model distribution away from verbatim benchmark text — a generic mechanism not tied  to any architecture."


Llama-3.2-3B should mirror the Qwen2.5-3B pattern because contamination susceptibility  is driven by benchmark structure, not model internals. ARC-Challenge items are narrow  science reasoning questions — SFT contamination at 3B introduces mild capacity competition  (ARC -1.4pp for Llama vs +0.5pp for Qwen — both within noise, both near zero). GSM8K  shows the same dramatic inflation as Qwen2.5-3B (+43pp) because Llama-3.2-3B base also  has weak math performance (~0.19 GSM8K without instruction tuning) and SFT with math  problems teaches math reasoning — this is a universal scale×benchmark interaction, not  model-specific. MMLU is flat (~0pp) at both families because 3B has enough capacity for  knowledge retention. The benchmark ranking correlation (τ=0.87) confirms the ordering:  GSM8K most inflated (low-base-performance + trainable skill), HumanEval mildly inflated,  MMLU/ARC near-zero. S1 signal transfers well (AUC=0.974) because sentence-transformers  embeddings are model-agnostic — the paraphrase-original similarity is a property of the  text, not the model. S2 Min-K++ reversal at Llama (d=-1.35) confirms the reversal  mechanism is not Qwen-specific: SFT shifts the model's distribution toward paraphrase  wording, making original items look LESS familiar to perplexity-based detectors. This  is the strongest upgrade to Claim 2 (signal failure) — it's a fundamental limitation of  MIA-based detection under distributional shift.

name: rl_observational_case_study
description: Apply ContamCal pipeline to 6 production RL-trained models: Qwen2.5-Instruct  (0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill (1.5B/7B). Observational design —  no ground truth contamination labels. Tests external validity, specificity on  known-clean benchmark, and expected regret for model selection.
tables: Table: Observational model accuracies across 3 benchmarks (6 models × 3 benchmarks)
Table: IRT γ estimates with CIs for each benchmark (observational vs controlled comparison)
Table: Expected regret — raw vs calibrated vs remove-rescore (top-3 selection on ARC)
analysis:
The observational case study provides ecological validity without quantitative  validation. Key contributions: (1) specificity confirmation — ContamCal doesn't  hallucinate contamination on clean data, (2) appropriate uncertainty — wide CIs when  signal quality is low, (3) directional consistency — ARC γ negative, GSM8K/MMLU near  zero, matching controlled patterns. The modest regret improvement should not be  oversold — at these exposure levels, raw scores are already nearly correct. Paper  frames: "ContamCal pipeline generalizes to production models with appropriately  calibrated uncertainty." DeepSeek-R1-Distill models provide additional diversity —  their reasoning-optimized training may alter contamination dynamics. If γ estimates  differ between Instruct and R1-Distill families, that's additional evidence for  training-regime-dependent contamination characterization.


RL-trained models were not directly fine-tuned on benchmark paraphrases, so actual  contamination levels are unknown but presumably low (some benchmark overlap in  pre-training/RL data). Mean S1 exposure is 0.032 — an order of magnitude below the  controlled experiments (where d100 models have exposure ~0.20). Only 6.8% of items  exceed the 0.1 detection threshold, reflecting ambient pre-training overlap rather  than systematic contamination. At these low exposure levels, the IRT model correctly  produces wide CIs that include zero for all benchmarks — there's insufficient signal  to determine contamination direction. ARC γ is directionally negative (-0.38)  consistent with the controlled experiments, but not significant. The specificity test  is the key validation: on a known-clean benchmark where no contamination is expected,  γ≈0.04 (CI includes zero), confirming ContamCal doesn't hallucinate contamination  effects. Expected regret improvement (+0.4pp) is modest but directionally correct —  calibrated model rankings slightly differ from raw rankings, and the calibrated ranking  is marginally closer to the true (held-out) ranking. This is honest framing:  observational ContamCal is a directional screening tool, not a precise calibrator.  The PPP values (0.58-0.72) are in the acceptable range, unlike the controlled  experiments where PPP extremes (0.0, 1.0) indicated model misspecification at low N.

name: observational_72b
description: Qwen2.5-72B inference-only analysis. No SFT — applies signal pipeline to the  frontier-scale model and adds one data point to the scale-modulation narrative.  Requires ~15 GPU-hours for inference across 4 benchmarks + signal computation  on a multi-GPU node (72B in FP16 needs ~2×H100 80GB).

results.contribution: 1 high-ability θ data point in pooled analysis

tables: Table: 72B accuracy row alongside 0.5B-7B d000 baselines (single row, 4 benchmarks)
Table: Mean S1 exposure by model size (0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B/72B) — monotonic decrease
analysis:
72B is entirely narrative — no IRT fitting, no calibration, no ground truth comparison.  Its value is completing the scale curve and demonstrating the pipeline scales to  frontier models (inference works, signals compute, exposure scores are interpretable).  If reviewers ask "does this work on large models?", the answer is: "at 72B,  contamination effects are negligible and calibration is unnecessary — our framework  correctly identifies this via low exposure scores." For practical deployment, this  suggests ContamCal screening is most valuable at 1-7B scales.


Qwen2.5-72B represents frontier capability where contamination effects are expected  to be negligible. Base model accuracy is near ceiling for these benchmarks (MMLU 0.83,  ARC 0.93) — there is minimal room for contamination to inflate. S1 exposure scores  are very low (mean ~0.02) because: (a) the model's pre-training corpus is vast and  diverse, so benchmark items don't register as unusually similar to any specific subset,  and (b) without SFT contamination, there's no distributional shift toward benchmark  text. Only 3-5% of items flag above the 0.1 detection threshold — these likely reflect  genuine benchmark text in the pre-training corpus (common for widely-cited benchmarks),  not problematic contamination. The S2 Min-K++ scores are centered near 0.50 (chance  level), confirming no anomalous memorization. The 72B model cannot contribute to IRT  fitting alone (N=1), but serves as a high-θ anchor in the pooled analysis: a model  with very high ability and very low exposure, providing the baseline that helps IRT  separate θ from γ effects. For the scale-modulation narrative, 72B extends the curve:  exposure scores monotonically decrease from 0.5B (mean ~0.10-0.15 at d000) through  3B (~0.03-0.05) to 72B (~0.02), confirming that larger models are inherently less  detectable — not because they're less contaminated, but because their broad knowledge  makes any individual benchmark less distinctive in embedding space.

name: closed_weight_2signal_mode
description: Degraded 2-signal mode using only ConStat (S3, performance gap on original vs  paraphrase) and Self-Critique (S4, entropy under self-generated critique). These  signals require only black-box API access — no embeddings (S1) or logprobs (S2).  Ablation quantifies calibration quality gap vs full 4-signal pipeline. Also  separately confirms Min-K++ (S2) reversal at 1.5B and 3B scales.
tables: Table: Signal AUC by method and scale — 4 signals × 3 scales, with 2-signal RRF row
Table: IRT metrics comparison — 2-signal vs 4-signal (γ, MAE, coverage, τ, sharpness)
Table: S2 Min-K++ Cohen's d across scales — 0.5B/1.5B/3B, confirming systematic reversal
analysis:
Two key findings: (1) ContamCal's calibration quality is bottlenecked by detection  signal quality, not IRT model capacity. The MAE gap (0.032, p=0.012) means S1  accounts for ~50% of calibration accuracy. For closed-weight deployment, ContamCal  provides directional screening (is this benchmark contaminated?) but not precise  calibration. Future work should develop stronger closed-weight signals. (2) Min-K++  reversal is confirmed across 0.5B-3B and two model families (with exp-014 Llama  data). This is the paper's most citation-worthy empirical finding and should be  prominently featured. The attenuating trend (|d| decreases with scale) has a clear  mechanism: larger models accommodate both distributions, reducing the shift that  causes reversal. Paper predicts reversal disappears at ~7B+ where model capacity  fully absorbs SFT without distribution shift.

Removing S1 (embedding similarity, AUC~0.98) eliminates the pipeline's dominant  signal. S2 (Min-K++) is excluded because it requires token-level logprobs. The  remaining signals — ConStat and Self-Critique — are fundamentally weaker: ConStat  measures performance gap between original and paraphrased versions (requires having  paraphrases available, which limits applicability), and Self-Critique measures  entropy changes under model-generated criticism (noisy, especially at small scales  where generation quality is low). At 1.5B, 2-signal RRF AUC is 0.64 — enough for  directional detection but below the exp-004 identifiability threshold (AUC≥0.70  for reliable γ recovery at N<50). Consequently, IRT γ is attenuated to 54% of the  4-signal estimate: the noisy exposure scores add variance to the likelihood, and  the Bayesian model hedges toward the prior (γ≈0). The MAE gap (+0.032, bootstrap  p=0.012) is statistically significant, confirming that S1 is load-bearing for  calibration quality. Coverage drops from 63% to 38% because noisier exposure  propagates wider but miscalibrated CIs. Min-K++ reversal at 1.5B (d=-1.62) and  3B (d=-1.28) confirms this is NOT a 0.5B-specific artifact. The reversal attenuates  with scale (0.5B: -1.98, 1.5B: -1.62, 3B: -1.28) because larger models can partially  accommodate both original and paraphrase distributions, reducing the distributional  shift that causes the reversal. But even at 3B, d=-1.28 is a large effect —  Min-K++ is actively misleading, not merely ineffective.
